newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iraqi group says Kurds and Baghdad in oil trade.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi group says Kurds and Baghdad in oil trade.

text.p: An Iraqi opposition group on Tuesday accused one of the main Kurdish militias in northern Iraq of making hundreds of thousands of dollars a day from trafficking in diesel fuel across the border into Turkey.
But Western sources close to northern Iraq say the figures are exaggerated.

The Iraqi National Congress (INC) said in a statement Iraq's oil ministry sells around eight million litres of diesel a day at 1.5 cents a litre to two companies, one controlled by the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and another by President Saddam Hussein's son, Uday.

The fuel is then sold to Turkish truckers at 11.5 cents per litre, which together with border duties on the fuel and various service charges exacted on the lorries, nets the KDP around $750,000 per day, an INC spokesman told Reuters.
"I'm not sure about (the figures). "It's more like several million (dollars) a month," a Western diplomat told Reuters.

The oil taken by truck across the Turkish border is outside the U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food agreement with Iraq whereby the Iraqi government was allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy urgently needed food and medicine.
"This is being carried out in violation of the sanctions and in full view of the international monitors observing the oil-for-food deal," an INC spokesman said.
Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990. But the Western allies that ousted Iraqi troops tacitly approve of a makeshift oil trade on the Turkish border.

Trucks are allowed by the Turkish authorities to bring back up to four tonnes of diesel from northern Iraq through the main crossing at Habur, in southeast Turkey. The diesel is then sold in Turkey at prices much lower than official Turkish levels.
Turkish officials said 260,000 vehicles, mostly trucks, made the crossing in 1995, the last year for which figures were immediately available.
The KDP denied the illegality of the trade.
"This accusation is totally baseless. Whatever is being done, is being done above board. This has been going on for the last five or six years," KDP spokesman, Safeen Dizayee told Reuters.

The sharing of revenues from the Turkish border has been one of the main bones of contention between the KDP and a rival faction in sporadic fighting since 1994. The Kurds have ruled northern Iraq under a Western air shield since the end of the 1991 Gulf War.
